theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

Make lots and lots of money from welding as soon as I can

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Set out a personal entrepreneurial strategy for a Level 3 welder who wants to own a small fabrication shop in four years. Give goals and milestones for each year.
essays.modelAnswer: My goal is to own a fabrication shop in Clarendon with two staff, making gates, grills and railings, within four years. In year 1 I keep my job, gain my welding qualifications for pipe and stainless, and save a set amount each month in a separate account. I start a skills audit and take a short course in bookkeeping. In year 2 I do small weekend jobs, registered under a business name, to build a customer list and learn pricing. I keep job cards and photos. I study the market and choose my niche. In year 3 I write a business plan with a cash flow forecast, buy the main tools with savings, and find a shop space. I talk to a mentor and a lender. In year 4 I leave my job, open the shop, hire a helper when the work is steady, and review my plan every three months.
markingPoints: Clear, measurable, dated main goal
Year 1: skills, qualifications and savings
Year 2: small jobs, registration, records and market study
Year 3: business plan, equipment, premises, support
Year 4: launch, hiring when steady, regular review

essays.stem: Carry out a personal SWOT analysis for a welder who wants to start a business making and fitting gates, grills and railings, and explain how it shapes the strategy.
essays.modelAnswer: Strengths: a Level 3 certificate, years of site experience, good welding and fitting skills, and contacts with builders. Weaknesses: little experience of pricing, bookkeeping or selling, and small savings. Opportunities: new housing schemes nearby, home owners who want security grills, and hotels that need railings. Threats: cheap imported ready-made grills, rising steel prices, rival shops and late-paying customers. The SWOT shapes the strategy. The welder should build on the strengths by using builder contacts and quality as the selling point. Weaknesses are fixed by a bookkeeping course and a mentor, and by saving before starting. The housing opportunity suggests a niche in security grills and gates for new homes. Threats are reduced by offering made-to-measure work that imports cannot match, short quotation validity, and deposits.
markingPoints: Relevant strengths
Relevant weaknesses
Relevant opportunities
Relevant threats
Explains how each part shapes the strategy

essays.stem: Explain how to choose a niche for a new fabrication business, and how market research would test it.
essays.modelAnswer: A niche is a small, special part of the market that a business serves better than others. To choose one, the welder lists what he does best, such as stainless steel or pipe work, and the needs he sees, such as hotels wanting railings or farms needing water tank stands. He looks for work where there are few good rivals and customers will pay for quality. He then tests the idea with market research. He counts the rival shops and visits them to see their prices and how long customers wait. He talks to builders, hotel maintenance managers or farmers and asks what they buy, how often and what problems they have. He may do a short survey or take a few trial jobs. If the research shows steady demand and fair prices, the niche is worth starting. If not, he changes the idea.
markingPoints: Explains what a niche is
Matches own skills to needs seen
Looks for few rivals and good prices
Market research: rivals, customers, survey or trial jobs
Uses results to decide or change the idea

essays.stem: Explain how a fabricator should build up the price of a steel staircase job. Use a worked example with materials, consumables, labour, overheads, profit and GCT 'at the current rate'.
essays.modelAnswer: First list the materials from the drawing: for example, steel and plate for J$120 000. Add consumables such as rods, discs, gas and paint, say J$15 000. Work out labour: 40 hours at J$1 500 is J$60 000. The direct cost is 120 000 + 15 000 + 60 000 = J$195 000. Next add a share of overheads, such as rent, power, insurance and the van. If the shop adds 15%, that is J$29 250, making J$224 250. Then add profit, say 10% of that, J$22 425, to give J$246 675 before tax. A small contingency may be added for risk. If the shop is registered for GCT, GCT is added at the current rate on top of this price. The quotation states what is included and excluded, the payment terms and how long the price is valid. The price is checked against what rivals charge.
markingPoints: Materials and consumables listed and costed
Labour hours times rate; direct cost totalled
Overheads added
Profit (and contingency) added, sums correct
GCT at the current rate if registered; quote terms; market check

essays.stem: Explain how to work out the break-even point for a fabrication shop, and how the owner can use it to make decisions.
essays.modelAnswer: First the owner adds up the fixed costs for a month, the costs that stay the same however much work is done: rent, insurance, loan repayments, the owner's wage and the phone. Then, for a typical job, he takes the variable costs, such as steel, rods and labour for that job, away from the price. What is left is the contribution each job makes towards fixed costs. The break-even point is the fixed costs divided by the contribution per job. For example, if fixed costs are J$200 000 a month and each gate leaves J$25 000, the shop must sell 8 gates a month to break even. The owner can use this to set sales targets, check whether a price is high enough, see the effect of a rent rise or a new machine, and decide whether the business idea is realistic before starting.
markingPoints: Fixed costs identified and totalled
Contribution per job explained
Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution
Correct worked example
Uses: targets, pricing, effect of changes, testing the idea

essays.stem: Describe the steps to set up a fabrication business legally in Jamaica, including registration, tax and the duties of an employer.
essays.modelAnswer: The owner chooses a structure: a sole trader, a partnership or a limited company. A business name or company is registered with the Companies Office of Jamaica. The owner needs a TRN for tax and registers the business with Tax Administration Jamaica. He keeps records and files income tax returns. If sales pass the set level, he registers for GCT and charges it at the current rate. For government jobs he will need a tax compliance certificate. He checks with the parish council that the shop space may be used for fabrication. He takes out insurance, such as public liability and property cover. When he hires staff, he gives them written terms, registers as an employer, makes the statutory payroll deductions and pays them over on time. He must also provide a safe workplace, safe machines, PPE and training.
markingPoints: Chooses a structure and registers the name or company
TRN, tax registration, records and returns
GCT registration when required; TCC for government work
Premises use and insurance
Employer duties: terms, payroll deductions, safety

essays.stem: Compare three ways to pay for the start-up equipment of a welding shop (savings, a loan and hire purchase or leasing), giving an advantage and a disadvantage of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Using personal savings means there is no interest to pay and no debt, and the owner keeps full control. The disadvantage is that savings take time to build, and once they are spent there is less cash for emergencies or slow months. A loan from a bank or credit union gives a large sum at once, so the shop can start sooner with good equipment. However, it must be repaid with interest every month, even when work is slow, and the lender may want security, such as a title. Hire purchase or leasing spreads the cost of a machine over time, and a lease may include servicing. The disadvantage is that the total cost is usually higher, and with a lease the shop may never own the machine. Many owners mix these: savings for tools and a deposit, and a loan or hire purchase for the large machines.
markingPoints: Savings: advantage and disadvantage
Loan: advantage and disadvantage
Hire purchase or leasing: advantage and disadvantage
Mentions interest, security or ownership correctly
Sensible conclusion or mix of methods

essays.stem: Describe the main risks to a new fabrication business (safety, cash flow, quality, steel prices and bad debts) and explain how the owner can control each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Safety: a burn, eye injury or fall can hurt a worker, stop work and lead to claims. The owner controls it with safe machines, PPE, training, fire extinguishers and insurance. Cash flow: the shop may run short of cash while waiting to be paid. The owner uses a cash flow forecast, takes deposits and stage payments, and keeps a cash reserve. Quality: a poor weld or a gate that does not fit can lose customers and need costly rework. The owner follows drawings, checks work before delivery and trains staff. Steel prices: a rise can wipe out the profit on a quoted job. The owner gives quotes a short validity, buys steel early and adds a small contingency. Bad debts: a customer may never pay. The owner checks new customers, uses written contracts, invoices promptly and follows up overdue accounts.
markingPoints: Safety risk and controls
Cash flow risk and controls
Quality risk and controls
Steel price risk and controls
Bad debt risk and controls

essays.stem: Explain how a fabrication shop can win and keep customers through marketing, quotations and service.
essays.modelAnswer: To win customers, the shop decides who its customers are, such as builders, home owners or hotels, and what makes it different, for example galvanised gates fitted within ten days. It shows photos of past work on social media and in a small folder, visits building sites, and asks happy customers to tell others. It puts its name on its van and on finished work. Quotations are clear, written and given quickly. They list what is included and left out, the price, payment terms and how long the price stands. Customers are kept by doing what was promised: good welding, accurate fitting, a clean site and work finished on time. Any extra work is agreed in writing. Problems are fixed quickly and politely. The shop follows up after a job, asks for feedback and keeps in touch, so customers return and refer others.
markingPoints: Knows its customers and its selling point
Uses suitable marketing: photos, site visits, word of mouth
Clear, prompt written quotations with terms
Delivers quality on time; agrees extras in writing
Handles problems and follows up for repeat work

essays.stem: Explain how and how often an owner should review a personal entrepreneurial strategy, and which measures show whether it is working.
essays.modelAnswer: The owner should review the strategy at set times, for example every three months, and also when something big changes, such as losing a large customer or a steep rise in steel prices. He compares what has happened with the goals and dates in his plan. Useful measures are sales against the target, profit on each finished job compared with its quote, cash in the bank and money owed to the shop, the number of repeat and referred customers, and how many jobs are finished on time. He also checks his personal goals: savings, new skills or qualifications gained, and hours worked. If a measure is off track, he finds the reason and changes the plan, for example by repricing, changing the niche, or getting more training. He writes the changes down with new dates, so the strategy stays a working plan.
markingPoints: Regular reviews and reviews after big changes
Compares results with goals and dates
Business measures: sales, profit per job, cash, debtors
Customer and personal measures
Finds causes, changes the plan and records new dates

practical1.title: Personal SWOT, niche test and four-year strategy poster for a fabrication business
practical1.brief: Each member first completes a personal skills audit and a personal SWOT on the forms the assessor gives, thinking about running their own fabrication business. Then, as a group, choose one niche for a small fabrication business in a Jamaican town you know (for example, security grills for new homes, water tank stands for farms or railings for hotels). Test the idea: each member asks at least three possible customers or suppliers (builders, home owners, hardware stores or hotel staff, in person or by phone) the short survey questions the group writes, and records the answers. Share the roles: team leader, survey writer, recorder of results, poster designer and presenter (with five members), or combine roles for four. Together, draw up a four-year strategy poster: the main goal with a date, yearly milestones (skills, savings, registration, equipment, premises, first hire), the niche and why the survey supports it, and the main risks with controls. Present the poster to the assessor in 5–10 minutes; every member speaks. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the audits, SWOTs, survey results and poster once for the whole group.
materials: Skills audit and SWOT forms (from the assessor)
Survey sheet template and pens; a phone if members call people
Flip chart paper or poster card, markers and a ruler
photos: Each member's completed skills audit and SWOT
checklist: Completed an honest personal skills audit and SWOT
Asked at least three people the survey questions and recorded the answers
Helped choose a niche and linked it to the survey results
Contributed SMART yearly milestones to the poster
Named at least one risk and a sensible control
Spoke clearly in the presentation and answered a question
safety: Treat survey answers and personal SWOTs as private; use first names only
Be polite and respectful to people surveyed; stop if they do not wish to answer
Survey in public or at the Centre, in pairs, and not after dark
Share the workload fairly within the group

practical2.title: Costed quotation, break-even and 12-month cash flow forecast for a small fabrication shop, presented at a role-played loan meeting
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a pack: a sketch of a steel staircase or a set of security grills, a price list for steel and consumables (J$ prices made up for the exercise), the shop's monthly fixed costs, and a loan offer. Share the roles: estimator, costing checker, cash flow writer, business plan writer and presenter (combine roles for four members). As a group: (1) cost the job from the sketch and write a quotation with materials, consumables, labour, overheads, profit and GCT 'at the current rate' (the assessor gives the rate), plus what is included and left out, payment terms and validity; (2) work out the shop's break-even point in jobs per month; (3) write a 12-month cash flow forecast for the shop, including the loan and its repayments; (4) write a one-page business plan summary. Then hold a 10-minute role-played loan meeting with the assessor as the loan officer, using the forecast to show when the loan can be repaid. Every member answers at least one question. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in all the papers once for the whole group.
materials: Assessor's pack: job sketch, price list, fixed costs and loan offer
Blank quotation, break-even and cash flow forms, or a computer with a spreadsheet
A table and chairs set up for the loan meeting
photos: The costing sheet for the job with workings
The 12-month cash flow forecast (paper or screen)
The role-played loan meeting in progress
checklist: Costed materials, consumables and labour correctly
Added overheads, profit and GCT at the rate given
Worked out the break-even point correctly
Built a cash flow forecast that includes the loan repayments
Wrote or checked part of the business plan summary
Answered the loan officer's question clearly and honestly
safety: The figures are for training only; do not share real personal financial details
Keep the role play respectful and professional
Back up spreadsheet work and close files containing personal details
Share the workload fairly and take a short break if needed
